lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the twenty sixth of February, eighteen eighty five, fourteen governments signed a General Act at Berlin. It names no border and gives no territory to anyone.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Six documents, no border, and nobody from Africa in the room.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Scramble for Africa. Eighteen eighty four to nineteen fourteen.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Berlin, the fifteenth of November, eighteen eighty four. In eighteen seventy Europe held about ten per cent of Africa.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Otto von Bismarck, the German Chancellor, opens a conference on Africa at his residence: fourteen governments, European and American, and no African of any kind.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It writes the rules by which a European power may claim African land; within thirty years, by the event record, those powers hold over ninety per cent of it.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the twentieth, in London, Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice, answering for the Foreign Office in the House of Commons, is asked about Portugal's claims on the Congo, the great river of Central Africa.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice, to the House.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: I have already stated that the decision of territorial claims is not among the bases of the Conference.

segments.author: Lord Edmond Fitzmaurice
segments.work: answer to Jacob Bright in the House of Commons, Hansard

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Two articles set rules for future occupations on the coasts: whoever takes a coast must establish authority there.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: G. N. Uzoigwe, in the UNESCO General History of Africa, written by African historians, read it this way.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: This was the so-called doctrine of effective occupation that was to make the conquest of Africa such a murderous business.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Six documents, no border, and nobody from Africa in the room.

segments.author: G. N. Uzoigwe
segments.work: European partition and conquest of Africa, in the UNESCO General History of Africa, volume seven

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Matabeleland, in what is now Zimbabwe, the thirtieth of October, eighteen eighty eight. Lobengula, king of the Ndebele, grants a concession, a right to dig, to the British South Africa Company of Cecil Rhodes, Prime Minister of the Cape Colony.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Told what he has granted, the king sends two messengers to find out whether England exists and has a queen.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: They carry a letter. Lobengula, to Queen Victoria, as Henry Labouchere, a member of Parliament, read it to the House in eighteen ninety three.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: A document was read and presented to me for signature. I asked what it contained, and was told that in it were my words and the words of those men. I put my hand to it.

segments.author: Lobengula
segments.work: letter to Queen Victoria, as Henry Labouchere read it to the House of Commons

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: On the tenth of August Lobengula writes again.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: If the Queen hears that I have given away the whole country it is not so. I have no one in my country who knows how to write.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In October, Labouchere told the House, the Company received a royal charter to govern the land, with no further word to Lobengula. In eighteen ninety three its guns settled it, by the event record; the country became Rhodesia.

segments.author: Lobengula
segments.work: second letter to Queen Victoria, as Labouchere read it to the House of Commons

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Hornkrans, in what is now Namibia, the thirtieth of May, eighteen ninety. Hendrik Witbooi, chief of the Witbooi Nama, has learned that Maharero, chief of the Herero, has given himself into German protection.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The two peoples are at war; Witbooi writes to his enemy anyway.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Hendrik Witbooi, to Maharero, rendered by Void from his Cape Dutch.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: you will have everlasting regret, that you have given your land and your right of government into the hands of the white people

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A German proclamation of December nineteen oh five says Witbooi has been killed by a German bullet.

segments.author: Hendrik Witbooi (Void translation from the Cape Dutch)
segments.work: letter to Maharero, chief of the Herero, rendered by Void from the Cape Dutch

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Congo, nineteen oh three. The Congo Free State, which governs the river basin, is the personal colony of Leopold the Second, King of Belgium, by the event record; its people must bring in rubber.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In May the House of Commons asks the Government to confer with the other signatories of the Berlin Act; that year Roger Casement, the British consul, goes up the river.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A girl his report calls T seven tells him what the soldiers did at her village. Casement sets it down in the third person.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: they began catching and tying the people, and killed lots of them.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At Lake Mantumba the consul saw a boy of eleven or twelve whose right hand had been cut off at the wrist.

segments.author: Roger Casement
segments.work: the statement of a girl the report calls T 7, as the consul set it down in the third person, Africa No. 1 (1904)

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Free State sends its own commission. It finds women held as hostages for the rubber, a practice the State had forbidden and could not suppress, and the river emptied.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Then it sets every such cause below smallpox and sleeping sickness.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: All of these causes of depopulation are secondary in importance.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The two records agree on the hostages and divide on what the people died of. In nineteen oh eight, by the event record, the king was made to hand the Congo to Belgium.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Namibia, then a German colony, nineteen oh four. The Herero have risen. Daniel Kariko, an under-chief, swore afterwards to the cause, before the British administration that followed.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Daniel Kariko, on oath.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Our people were compelled to work on farms, and the farmers had them chained up by the police and flogged without mercy for the slightest little thing.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: A German who shot the daughter of a chief was declared not guilty, he said. That decided them for war.

segments.author: Daniel Kariko
segments.work: affidavit sworn before the Union administration at Windhuk, in the Report on the Natives of South-West Africa

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The second of October. Lothar von Trotha, commanding the German troops, signs a proclamation to the Herero people, here in the English of David Ciarlo.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Any Herero found within the German frontier, with or without a gun, with or without cattle, will be shot.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: An addendum tells the troops how to read it.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: the shooting at women and children is to be understood as shooting above their heads, so as to force them to flee.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It assumes that no more male prisoners will be taken.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Gottlob Kamatoto, a Herero who served a German officer, swore that seven Herero leaders came in to discuss peace and at sunset were tied with ropes, led aside and shot.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In December nineteen oh five a new governor called the survivors in; those who came went to the camps.

segments.author: General Lothar von Trotha
segments.work: proclamation to the Herero people and addendum to the troops, Osombo-Windhuk, in David Ciarlo's English translation for German History in Documents and Images

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Windhuk, nineteen eighteen, under a British administration now. Nobody knows how many Herero died; what exists is a set of counts of unlike things.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The administration at Windhuk, in its report.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Out of between 80,000 and 90,000 souls only about 15,000 starving and fugitive Hereros were alive at the end of 1905, when von Trotha relinquished his task.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: In two thousand and four the research service of the German parliament counted seven thousand six hundred and eighty two prisoners dead in the camps.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It put the entire people at thirty five to a hundred thousand before the war and fourteen to twenty five thousand after. The event record says sixty five thousand of eighty thousand. This programme states no single number.

segments.author: The Administrator's Office, Windhuk
segments.work: Report on the Natives of South-West Africa and their Treatment by Germany, Cd. 9146

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Five accounts of what was done and what to call it, argued from what this programme could read: the Act, parliamentary papers, three rulers' letters, a consul's report, the Free State's own inquiry, a German order and a German parliament's paper.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The standard books, and the concession Lobengula signed, could not be read here. Each gets its own case first.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The first account is the case Europe made for itself: a treaty that binds the Powers to watch over the preservation of the native tribes, and a treatise.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Frederick Lugard, a British colonial governor, called it a dual mandate in nineteen twenty two.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: Let it be admitted at the outset that European brains, capital, and energy have not been, and never will be, expended in developing the resources of Africa from motives of pure philanthropy

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The second account is the rulers' own. Three speak here in their own words: two have been heard; the third kept his throne.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: At Adwa, on the first of March, eighteen ninety six, Menelik the Second, Emperor of Ethiopia, defeated the Italians, and Ethiopia kept its independence.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The next year Menelik wrote to James Rennell Rodd, with whom he had made a treaty in Amharic and English, on which text should settle a dispute. In the Foreign Office translation.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: let this translation, which is written in the French language, and which I enclose in this letter, be the witness between us, and if you accept this proposal, send me word of your acceptance by letter.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The third account holds that the Scramble was not an episode but a structure that outlived the flags.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Its texts are Walter Rodney on how Europe underdeveloped Africa, Frantz Fanon on the colonized, and Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's first president, who named the continuation neo-colonialism.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The UNESCO historians argue it from the conference itself. Uzoigwe, on what Berlin did.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: To all intents and purposes the appropriation of territory did take place at the conference and the question of future appropriation is clearly implied in its decisions.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fourth account follows the money through rubber, diamonds and copper; this programme holds documents for rubber alone.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The consul counted places he had known: Bolobo, a town on the upper Congo, fully forty thousand people once, believed to be seven or eight thousand.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Nothing in the primary record counts the territory entire. The historian Aldwin Roes, who names ten million as the campaign's figure, writes this.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: a firm estimate of the number of victims must indeed remain elusive

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The fifth account is the half the word leaves out. North Africa was taken by the same powers in the same decades.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The event record carries its resistance: Abd el-Kader, who fought the French in Algeria; the Mahdi, who took Khartoum in Sudan; Omar al-Mukhtar, who fought the Italians in Libya.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: It holds that this resistance drew on Islamic political and military traditions with no equivalent south of the Sahara.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The one North African document held is by Jules Ferry, a former premier of France, defending the conquest of Algeria in eighteen eighty five, rendered by Void from his French.

lines.speaker: M
lines.text: When we went to Algiers to destroy piracy and to secure the freedom of trade in the Mediterranean, were we doing the work of pirates, of conquerors, of devastators?

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The account answers with a count from the event record: an estimated eight hundred and twenty five thousand dead in the conquest of Algeria.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Each is true as far as it goes.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The colonizers leave out what their own records say was done in the basin the Act protected: the hostages, and the hands.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The rulers leave out the wars they fought with one another, and the rulers who did sign.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Pan African account leaves out what African governments did with the structure after independence.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The economic ledger leaves out the share of the dead the consul himself gave to disease.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: North Africa's own account leaves out the elites who worked with the powers it fought.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: And no Congolese, no North African, no Herero woman, no Nama survivor speaks here in their own words.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Fourteen governments signed the Act at Berlin in eighteen eighty five; no African was in the room. Within thirty years Europe held over ninety per cent of Africa; Ethiopia and Liberia alone were independent.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The Congo passed from its king to Belgium in nineteen oh eight. Germany recognised the Herero and Nama genocide in twenty twenty one, by the event record.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: The report that printed the Herero affidavits was withdrawn in nineteen twenty six from libraries throughout the British Empire; in South Africa and Namibia copies were destroyed.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: Six documents, no border, and nobody from Africa in the room.
